overview.title: 📖 Overview: Recast Vessels and Rainwater
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 16a–16b
overview.hebrewSource: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּשֶׁל צִיּוֹן הַמַּלְכָּה שֶׁעָשְׂתָה מִשְׁתֶּה לִבְנָהּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues untangling the halakhot of glass vessels, asking why a broken-and-recast glass vessel does not reassume its former impurity the way a metal vessel does. That leads into the story behind Shimon ben Shataḥ's decree on metal vessels — his own sister tried to dodge impurity by melting down her vessels — and into Abaye and Rava's two different explanations for that decree. The daf then turns to a mishna about vessels left under a drainpipe to catch rainwater, and closes by opening two further items on the list of eighteen decrees.

slides.title: 🔮 Glass Vessels: A Puzzle of 'Previous Impurity'
slides.subtitle: Why glass and metal behave differently once recast

nodes.content: ❓ If glass, like metal, can be melted and recast, shouldn't a remade glass vessel reassume its former impurity, the way metal does?
📜 Mishna on metal: broken = pure; remade into a new vessel = reverts to its old impurity
📜 Mishna on glass: broken = pure; remade into a new vessel = impure only from that point forward, never retroactively
✅ Resolved: glass's own impurity is only rabbinic, and 'previous impurity' is itself a rabbinic concept — the Sages did not stack one rabbinic decree atop another

callout.label: A further question:
callout.text: Shouldn't flat glass vessels at least become impure like flat metal ones (which are impure by Torah law)? No — the Sages deliberately spared them, so people would recognize glass's impurity as rabbinic and never burn teruma or consecrated food merely for touching it.

slides.title: 👑 Shel Tziyyon the Queen and the Melted Vessels
slides.subtitle: The incident behind Shimon ben Shataḥ's decree on metal
slides.hebrewSource: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּשֶׁל צִיּוֹן הַמַּלְכָּה שֶׁעָשְׂתָה מִשְׁתֶּה לִבְנָהּ
slides.label: The story:
slides.text: Shimon ben Shataḥ's sister, Shel Tziyyon the queen, made a wedding feast for her son. All her vessels became ritually impure, so she broke them, gave the pieces to a smith, and had him weld them into new vessels — hoping to escape the impurity entirely. The Sages ruled that the new vessels reassumed their previous impurity regardless. The reason: if people could simply break and recast an impure metal vessel to dodge the elaborate purification process for corpse-impurity — sprinkling the water of the red heifer on the third and seventh days — that entire mitzva would fall into disuse.

slides.title: 🤔 Abaye vs. Rava: Why Fear a Recast Metal Vessel?
slides.subtitle: Two rationales for the decree, tested by one case

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: The concern is that one may not perforate the vessel with a hole large enough to truly nullify it before recasting.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The concern is that people will conclude same-day immersion alone was sufficient to purify it, undermining the requirement to wait until nightfall.

lines.speaker: Test case
lines.text: If the vessel was broken completely, Abaye's concern no longer applies — the hole was certainly large enough.

lines.speaker: Still applies
lines.text: But Rava's concern remains even then, since onlookers might still conclude that same-day immersion alone had purified it.

slides.title: ☔ Vessels Under the Drainpipe — Deliberate or Forgotten?
slides.subtitle: Do they disqualify a ritual bath that fills from their overflow?
rows: A vessel catching rainwater under a drainpipe disqualifies a mikveh if it overflows into it — whether placed there deliberately or simply forgotten
Only a deliberately placed vessel disqualifies the mikveh; a forgotten one does not
They were counted in Ḥananya's attic and Beit Shammai's view prevailed — though Beit Shammai concedes a vessel forgotten in the courtyard itself (not under the pipe) stays pure
The dispute was never actually resolved — it still stands

callout.label: A finer point (school of Rav):
callout.text: All agree the water is unfit if the vessel was set out just as clouds were massing to rain, and fit if set out while clouds were scattering. They dispute only the case where clouds massed, scattered, and massed again before rain finally fell.

slides.title: 📋 Two More of the Eighteen Decrees
slides.subtitle: Completing Rabbi Yosei's shorter count, and opening a new topic

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: to complete Rabbi Yosei's tally, the daughters of the Samaritans (Kutim) were decreed to have the status of menstruants from the very cradle — issued on that same day
2️⃣ Another decree concerns any movable object the width of an ox-goad — it transmits corpse-impurity like a 'tent' over the dead
3️⃣ Rabbi Tarfon strongly objects: 'I will bury my sons if this is not a garbled halakha!' — insisting the ruling as commonly understood is wrong

4️⃣ As Rabbi Tarfon tells it, the true case was narrower: a farmer's ox-goad, resting on his shoulder with one end passing over a grave, itself becomes impure — but does not transmit impurity onward to anything else

summary.principle: The Sages calibrated each decree precisely to its purpose: glass, being only rabbinically impure, was spared the extra rabbinic layer of 'previous impurity' that metal vessels bear specifically to protect the red-heifer purification process from being circumvented.

flowSteps.content: 🔮 Glass vessels stay pure after being recast, since one rabbinic decree was not stacked on another
👑 Shel Tziyyon tried recasting to dodge impurity — the Sages ruled it does not work for metal

columns.content: 🤔 Abaye fears an insufficient hole; Rava fears people trusting same-day immersion
☔ Beit Hillel exempts a merely forgotten vessel under a drainpipe; Beit Shammai does not

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Even within the eighteen decrees, each ruling traces back to a precise, protective concern rather than sweeping stringency

quiz.q: Why does a broken-and-recast glass vessel NOT reassume its former impurity, unlike a metal vessel?
o: Because glass cannot actually be melted and recast
Because glass's basic impurity is only rabbinic, and 'previous impurity' is itself a rabbinic concept — the Sages did not stack one rabbinic decree on another
Because glass vessels are never impure at all
Because only priests use glass vessels
quiz.e: Since both glass's underlying impurity and the concept of 'previous impurity' are rabbinic, the Sages did not compound one rabbinic decree with another for glass.

quiz.q: Why did Shel Tziyyon the queen break and recast her impure vessels before her son's wedding feast, and what did the Sages rule?
o: She wanted more elaborate vessels; the Sages praised her
She hoped to escape their ritual impurity; the Sages ruled the new vessels reverted to their previous impurity anyway
She was required to do so by law; the Sages agreed the impurity was gone
She acted to honor Shimon ben Shataḥ; the Sages exempted her
quiz.e: Shel Tziyyon melted and recast her impure vessels hoping to purify them, but the Sages ruled that recast metal vessels reassume their previous impurity.

quiz.q: What is Rava's distinct reason for decreeing 'previous impurity' on recast metal vessels, as opposed to Abaye's reason?
o: That the metal itself is inherently dangerous
That people might conclude same-day immersion alone was sufficient to purify the vessel, undermining the requirement to wait until nightfall
That metal vessels are too expensive to purify properly
That recasting always leaves a vessel physically flawed
quiz.e: Rava worried that if a recast vessel appeared purified simply through immersion that same day, people would wrongly conclude same-day immersion suffices generally.

quiz.q: According to Beit Hillel, does a vessel merely forgotten (not deliberately placed) under a drainpipe disqualify a mikveh that fills partly from its overflow?
o: Yes, in all cases
No — only a deliberately placed vessel disqualifies the mikveh
Only if the vessel is made of stone
Only on Shabbat
quiz.e: Beit Hillel distinguishes intention from forgetfulness: only a vessel deliberately placed to catch rainwater disqualifies the mikveh, unlike Beit Shammai who forbids both cases.

quiz.q: What decree did Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak cite to complete Rabbi Yosei's shorter count of the eighteen decrees?
o: That glass vessels are impure
That the daughters of the Samaritans (Kutim) are considered menstruants from the cradle
That metal vessels reassume previous impurity
That a mikveh needs forty se'a of water
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak explained that the decree treating Samaritan daughters as menstruants from birth was also issued that day, completing the tally to eighteen even according to Rabbi Yosei's count.
